name: Etruscan Red
lede: Etruscan Red is a muted terracotta brown, first filed by Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary and, in Japan, carried under a different name tied to persimmon water.

sections.title: Filed in 1912, dated earlier
sections.body: Etruscan Red is first filed by Ridgway's 1912 "Color Standards and Color Nomenclature," plate XXVII, hue 5″, as a reddish terracotta brown [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name earlier still, to 1905, plate 4 G 11 [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed the same name in block 39 [2]. Our sources do not explain why the name invokes the Etruscans specifically [1]. The hex value, #AD6B60, comes from a scan of an aged printed plate and only approximates the original [1].

sections.title: In Japan: Mizugaki
sections.body: In Japan, the same hue is listed among the traditional colors as Mizugaki (水がき), "water persimmon" [3]. Its nearest named look-alikes in our library are [[copper-penny]], [[ocher-red]], [[cacao-brown]] and [[marsh-rose]], all within a few units of it [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this terracotta in 1.07 percent of the 23,781 paintings we have, 255 of them, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 99 [5]. That is more common than 59 percent of the named colors in our archive [5]. It peaks in the 1900s, 2.5 times the expected rate for that century, on 19 paintings [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 53 percent of the 99 paintings where it appears [5]. India is the most over-represented country for it, 2.5 times the expected rate, 23 of 721 paintings [5]. The earliest match in our archive is dated 1301, nearly six centuries before the name's earliest record; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [5].

origin.named_after: first filed by Ridgway's 1912 color dictionary; the Etruscan reference itself is undocumented in our sources
